title: Scaling Agentic Verifier for Competitive Coding
claim: Naively scaling random test inputs barely helps, while learned targeted inputs scale well and can rival or beat curated ground-truth inputs.
layout: 3 panels in a row sharing a legend, shaded confidence bands
description: A single row of three line plots, one for each benchmark: USACO, LiveCodeBench and OJBench. A shared legend sits on top. Blue is random generated input, red is verifier generated input, and green is ground truth input. In every panel the x-axis is the number of inputs (1, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64) and the y-axis is Best@K accuracy. Each curve is a line with dots and a translucent shaded band around it. The blue random curve starts lowest and stays nearly flat. The green and red curves rise steeply at first and then level off. In USACO the red curve passes above the green one, which stops at 16 inputs. In the other two panels the green curve stays above the red one. The eye goes first to the gap between the blue curve and the other two.
caption: Best-of-$N$ performance under input-only execution-based voting as the number of test inputs increases. We compare randomly generated inputs, ground-truth test inputs from the benchmark suites, and inputs generated by our trained agentic verifier. Ground-truth inputs consistently outperform random inputs by a large margin, indicating the inefficiency of naive random input scaling. Verifier-generated inputs significantly improve over random generation and even surpass ground-truth test cases on USACO, demonstrating stronger discriminative power.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong coding capabilities but still struggle to solve competitive programming problems correctly in a single attempt. Execution-based re-ranking offers a promising test-time scaling strategy, yet existing methods are constrained by either difficult test case generation or inefficient random input sampling. To address this limitation, we propose Agentic Verifier, an execution-based agent that actively reasons about program behaviors and searches for highly discriminative test inputs that expose behavioral discrepancies among candidate solutions. Through multi-turn interaction with code execution environments, the verifier iteratively refines the candidate input generator and produces targeted counterexamples rather than blindly sampling inputs. We train the verifier to acquire this discriminative input generation capability via a scalable pipeline combining large-scale data synthesis, rejection fine-tuning, and agentic reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across five competitive programming benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over strong execution-based baselines, achieving up to +10-15% absolute gains in Best@K accuracy. Further analysis reveals clear test-time scaling behavior and highlights the verifier's broader potential beyond reranking.
